palette.$description: Layer 1 primitives. Raw values only, no meaning attached. Component code never names these; it goes through the Layer 2 semantic aliases in tokens/semantic. Layer 1 is identical in every theme.

neutral.$description: Ink-and-navy ramp at hue ~250. Steps 2-4 are not tuned freely: they are the brand's own Ink Black, Prussian Blue and Oxford Navy, converted to OKLCH losslessly (round-trips back to the exact same sRGB hex). Chroma is real here, not a whisper — 0.03 to 0.10 through the dark end — because these are meant to read as blue, not as a tinted grey. It tapers back toward neutral above step 8 so text.primary stays a crisp near-white rather than a visibly blue one. Step 1 is the darkest, step 12 the lightest, in both themes; it is the semantic layer that decides which end means 'background'.

1.$description: Sunken — darker than Ink Black itself, for what sits behind the base plane. Not one of the five named brand colors; derived by continuing the same ramp one step further down.

4.$description: Oxford Navy (#003566) — overlay surfaces (menus, popovers, dialogs).

amber.$description: The one accent that carries the brand — School Bus Yellow and Gold, used sparingly for signature moments and highlights against the ink-and-navy ramp above. Steps 1 to 6 are a monotonic ramp at the same hue family for tints, borders and text on light surfaces. The four named variants below are not ramp positions: solid and hover/text are the two brand yellows themselves (School Bus Yellow, Gold), converted losslessly from their hex values, not freely tuned.

solid.$description: School Bus Yellow (#ffc300) at full strength: a filled button, the active state of a control, the signature brand moment. Whatever sits on top of this is palette.amber.contrast, never white. See that token.

hover.$description: Gold (#ffd60a) — hover for a solid School-Bus-Yellow fill, and every other 'highlight' job (focus ring, active text, an icon that needs to pop). Brighter than solid, not darker: on a dark UI, lifting toward the light is what reads as 'closer to the pointer'.

text.$description: Gold again — amber as text or an icon color on a dark surface. Not for light surfaces; step 3 is the light-surface equivalent.

contrast.$description: The near-black-navy label that goes on top of amber.solid. THIS IS NOT A BUG AND MUST NOT BE 'FIXED' TO WHITE. School Bus Yellow at L 0.848 is a light color: white on it fails every contrast target there is, while this near-black lands well clear of 4.5:1. Every design system with a light-yellow primary has to make this call, and the label is the side that gives. Hued into the ink ramp (~250) rather than left neutral, so it reads as part of the same family instead of a flat grey stamped on top.

teal.$description: Cool counter-accent at hue ~190. Used sparingly, and never competing with amber for the same job. Its purpose is a second, orthogonal axis of meaning, not a second brand color.

1.$description: Only light theme uses this. Teal at step 2 clears 3:1 against a dark surface but lands near 2.2:1 against a near-white one, so light needs its own step.

track.$description: A categorical set, for things that differ in kind rather than in importance: a recorded track, a drum voice, a pad. These are the one place in the system where a colour carries identity instead of meaning, which is why they are a flat set rather than a ramp and why none of them is the brand. They sit at close to the same lightness so no track shouts louder than another, and far enough apart in hue to be told apart at the size of a five pixel bar.

danger.$description: Step 1 is for light theme, step 2 for dark. A status color has to be legible as text on whatever surface it lands on, and no single lightness manages that against both a near-black and a near-white background.

success.$description: Step 1 is for light theme, step 2 for dark. See danger.

alpha.$description: Translucent hairlines. Borders use these rather than an opaque neutral so that one border value reads correctly at every surface elevation instead of needing a variant per surface.
